analysis.one_liner: Sets consumer, worker, and pollution protections for states that deregulate electricity sales.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in the House Commerce Committee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was Rep. Dennis Kucinich's response to the 1990s push to let customers choose their electric company. It would have set a floor of protections that any state had to meet before or after deregulating retail electricity: clear billing and privacy rules, a ban on switching people's suppliers without permission, continued wages for utility workers when plants are sold, a fund for low-income customers' bills, a national renewable energy requirement, and new limits on pollution, including carbon dioxide. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential electricity customers would gain billing transparency, privacy for their usage data, protection from unauthorized supplier switches ("slamming") and unauthorized charges ("cramming"), dispute rights without forced arbitration, and no disconnection while a complaint is pending. Low- and moderate-income households would gain a new federal fund for affordable electric service, paid by a small wires charge on electricity carried over transmission lines. Utility workers would keep their pay and benefits for 30 months if their plant were sold, and could tap a retraining fund. People with rooftop solar would gain guaranteed net metering. The public would gain tighter pollution caps on power plants, including carbon dioxide and mercury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residential electricity customers, low-income households, utility workers

how_it_helps.text: States that deregulate retail electricity would have to give customers plain, itemized bills, written consent before their personal usage data is shared, a complaint process with no mandatory arbitration and no disconnection while a complaint is pending, and bans on 'slamming' (switching a customer's supplier without permission) and 'cramming' (billing for optional services without consent).

States would have to keep residential and industrial access charges within three percentage points of each other, ending a pattern where large industrial customers paid less per kilowatt-hour than households, and prohibiting any class of customers from being charged more than its proportional share of transmission and distribution costs.

A National Electric Public Benefit Fund, financed by a nonbypassable wires charge of at least 7 mills per kilowatt-hour, would help low- and moderate-income households afford electric service and would match state spending on workforce retraining, renewable energy, and conservation.

Utility workers would be guaranteed offers from a plant's buyer at no less than their existing wage rates and substantially equivalent benefits for at least 30 months after a sale, and generating plants would come under OSHA requirements with periodic government inspection.

The bill would ban consumer-funded bailouts of investor-owned power plants, require $2 billion per reactor in escrow for nuclear decommissioning and waste disposal, bar utility holding companies from owning unregulated businesses, cap any company at 20 percent of baseload, peaking, or ancillary-service plant categories in a deregulated state, and tighten antitrust review of utility mergers.

Power plants of 15 megawatts or more would face nationwide annual caps on nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide, mercury, and nuclear waste, with carbon dioxide falling from 1.71 billion tons in 2005 to 380 million tons by 2030, plus a renewable energy portfolio standard rising about 1 percent per year, net metering for rooftop solar and wind, and full fuel-source and emissions disclosure on every monthly bill.

Every state would be required to charter a Citizens' Utility Board to represent residential consumers before regulators and legislatures, and FERC would get a $10 million-a-year Office of the Consumer Counsel to argue the consuming public's side in federal proceedings.

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric utilities and their shareholders would bear most of the direct cost: the wires charge funding the public benefit fund, the $2 billion per reactor nuclear escrow, pollution caps, market-share limits, a ban on owning unregulated or foreign businesses, and mandatory divestiture of transmission and distribution assets in deregulating states. Some of these compliance costs would likely flow through to customers in rates, and the wires charge would appear on everyone's electric bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investor-owned electric utilities and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill is written as detailed command-and-control: federal mandates to set up state Citizens' Utility Boards, federal quality indexes, mandatory bill disclosures down to pie charts with prescribed colors, and a wires charge of at least 7 mills per kilowatt-hour that every electricity customer would pay. Its own sponsor estimated the consumer counsel office alone at $10 million a year, and the wires charge, escrows, and monitoring systems would add compliance costs that utilities would seek to recover in rates.

The 20 percent cap on generation ownership in any plant category, the forced transfer of transmission and distribution assets away from utilities within a year of state deregulation, and the flat ban on utilities owning any unregulated business would have forced sweeping restructurings of major companies, raising the risk of transition disruption and litigation rather than lower prices.

Advocates of competition argued at the time that letting customers choose suppliers and letting companies merge or diversify would lower prices faster than a new layer of federal regulation; this bill would have attached those controls permanently, and a good-faith critic could reasonably worry the protections would slow the very competition meant to discipline rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer, worker, and environmental protections are real and aimed at a genuine problem: deregulated retail electricity markets invited unauthorized switching, confusing bills, market power in generation, and stranded costs charged to ratepayers, while states varied widely in protecting anyone. The bill's cost is a heavy, prescriptive federal apparatus — a wires charge on every kilowatt-hour, mandated state institutions, ownership caps, and forced divestitures — that even sympathetic readers would call rigid, and its carbon caps were far more aggressive than any U.S. law then contemplated. On balance it clearly traded utility shareholder profits for household protections, and its design flaws are about heaviness and rigidity, not about who it serves.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee for less than three months and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on October 10, 1998, near the end of the second session of the 105th Congress, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day, and on October 21 it was referred again to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing or a vote, and the 105th Congress expired on January 3, 1999, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investor-owned electric utilities and their shareholders came out ahead: none of the wires charges, nuclear escrows, ownership caps, or forced divestitures was ever imposed, and the states and Congress that pursued deregulation in those years did so without this bill's consumer, worker, and environmental conditions.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as a consumer, worker, and environmental counterweight to electricity deregulation; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 10, 1998 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Energy and Power
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 21, 1998 and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Investor-owned electric utility industry
against.what_they_did: During the 1990s electricity restructuring debate, major utilities lobbied Congress for market-opening legislation without the consumer, worker, and environmental conditions this bill would have attached to deregulation.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill drew zero cosponsors of either party, so the only recorded positions are the Democratic sponsor's support and the Republican-led committee's inaction.

industries.note: The bill would bar utilities from charging customers for power plant bailouts, from owning unregulated or foreign businesses, and from cross-subsidizing affiliates; it would force divestiture of transmission and distribution assets within a year of state deregulation and cap any company at 20 percent of a plant category. Its shareholders bear the direct cost; the bill exists precisely because households in a deregulated market were expected to bear the risks otherwise.

Combustion plants of 15 megawatts or more would face annual nationwide caps on nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide, with the carbon cap falling roughly 78 percent by 2030, plus continuous emissions monitoring. Cheaper, dirtier generation would lose its cost advantage over cleaner sources.

Each licensed investor-owned reactor would have to escrow $1 billion for decommissioning and $1 billion for high- and low-level waste disposal, and the bill would cap the production of nuclear waste in curies per kilowatt-hour. This would shift disposal risk from future taxpayers and ratepayers back to the plant owners.

A federal renewable portfolio standard rising about one percentage point per year, guaranteed net metering for rooftop systems up to 2 megawatts, and mandated interconnection would create a growing market for wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, and landfill-gas generation.

The bill would let suppliers compete for customers in deregulating states — a genuine opening for new entrants — but would hold them to licensing, disclosure, anti-slamming and anti-cramming rules, and credit-discrimination laws. Their gain in market access comes wrapped in consumer protections they would rather not carry.
